subject: Art & Design
title: Jakob's Law: Users Prefer Familiar Patterns
description: A quick, practical guide to Jakob's Law: Users Prefer Familiar Patterns.

hook.text: Users spend most of their time on OTHER sites. They expect your site to work like those.

buildup.text: Jakob's Law: users transfer expectations from one product to another. Familiarity reduces learning effort.

discovery.text: E-commerce sites put the cart top-right. Search bars sit top-center. Logos link to home. These are learned conventions.

twist.text: Innovation vs. convention is a constant tension. Too innovative = confusing. Too conventional = forgettable.

climax.text: Jakob's Law matters because clearer reasoning leads to better judgments.

punchline.text: Don't make users learn your interface.

quiz.question: What does Jakob's Law suggest about website design?
options: Users expect your site to work like other sites they already use
Every website should look completely unique
Users prefer sites with the most features

details.summary: Jakob's Law states that users spend most of their time on other websites and therefore expect your site to work like those sites. Familiar patterns — search bars at the top, logos that link home, shopping carts in the upper right — reduce learning costs and cognitive effort.
details.whyItMatters: Innovation in interface conventions often harms usability. Jakob's Law argues for leveraging existing mental models rather than inventing new paradigms, because users bring expectations from every other site they've visited.
takeaways: Users expect your site to work like other familiar sites
Standard patterns reduce learning cost and cognitive effort
Interface innovation often harms rather than helps usability

faq.question: Does Jakob's Law mean you should never innovate?
faq.answer: It means innovate with caution. When you change conventions, users must relearn, which creates friction. Innovation is justified when the new pattern is significantly better — the iPhone's touch interface was unfamiliar but revolutionary. For incremental improvements, stick with conventions.

faq.question: What are the most ingrained web conventions?
faq.answer: Logos in the upper left linking to home, shopping cart in the upper right, hamburger menu for mobile navigation, blue underlined links, search bars at the top, and forms with labels above fields. Deviating from these forces users to think about navigation instead of content.
